name: Avogadro's Law
statement: Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of molecules.
meaning: At a fixed temperature and pressure, a gas's volume depends only on how many molecules it contains, not on what they are. Double the amount of gas and you double the volume; the identity, size, and mass of the molecules do not matter.
mechanism: Treating the gas as ideal — molecules effectively point-like, with negligible forces between them — every gas at the same temperature has the same average molecular kinetic energy, so the same number of molecules in the same volume exerts the same pressure regardless of species. It is the 'amount of gas' term isolated from the combined gas relations, and with Boyle's, Charles's, and Gay-Lussac's laws it assembles into the ideal gas law.

examples.text: One mole of an ideal gas occupies about 22.4 litres at 0 °C and one atmosphere — the classic figure, though its exact value depends on which standard conditions are used.
Adding more gas — more molecules — increases the volume proportionally at fixed temperature and pressure, which is why a balloon expands as you blow into it.
Because equal volumes hold equal numbers of molecules, the volume ratios of reacting gases equal their molecule ratios — two volumes of hydrogen and one of oxygen give two of water vapour.

variants.name: The ideal gas law
variants.text: PV = nRT, the unified relation of which Avogadro's law is the constant-temperature, constant-pressure piece linking volume to amount.

variants.name: The Avogadro constant
variants.text: A distinct concept named later: the number of particles per mole, about 6.022 × 10²³, coined 'Avogadro's number' by Jean Perrin in 1909. Avogadro stated the law but never measured this number.

whyItMatters: It supplied the crucial link between the volume of a gas and the count of its molecules, making sense of the whole-number ratios seen in gas reactions and underpinning the mole — the chemist's unit of amount. Long ignored, its revival was what finally let chemists agree on atomic and molecular weights.

working.text: at fixed temperature and pressure, treat volume as proportional to the number of moles, so V₁/n₁ = V₂/n₂.

working.lead: Keep the law and the constant apart
working.text: the law is a proportionality about gas volume; the Avogadro constant is a separate number of particles per mole named a century later.
apply it where the gas is dilute — moderate pressure, not-too-low temperature — and expect deviations otherwise.

limits: It is an idealisation exact only for ideal gases. Real gases deviate, significantly at high pressure and low temperature, because molecules have finite volume and exert attractive and repulsive forces. It remains a good approximation under ordinary conditions. It must also not be conflated with the Avogadro constant, a separate quantity named long after the law and never determined by Avogadro himself.
misreadings: It is not the same thing as 'Avogadro's number' — the law is a statement about gas volumes, the constant a count of particles per mole named by Perrin in 1909. And it is not exact for real gases; it holds in the ideal-gas limit and only approximately elsewhere.
origin: Proposed as a hypothesis by the Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro in 1811, explaining Gay-Lussac's combining-volume data. It was largely ignored for decades until Stanislao Cannizzaro's 1858 pamphlet, circulated at the 1860 Karlsruhe Congress, revived it and resolved the confusion over atomic weights.

sources.text: Avogadro's law, Wikipedia. — the statement, the ideal-gas mechanism, and the Cannizzaro revival.
Avogadro constant, Wikipedia. — the law-versus-constant distinction and Perrin's 1909 naming.
